title: A poor childhood
hook: his father died young, and as a boy he worked in a hospital for the poor in Medina del Campo

segments.voice: Yesterday, little Seneca: the small friar Teresa teased as half a friar. Today, we go back to where John started, and it's not a pretty place.

A young man from a comfortable family falls in love with a poor girl who weaves silk for a living. His family says: marry her, and you're out. He marries her anyway, and they're cut off. They have three sons. They're poor, but they're together. Then, when the youngest is still a toddler, the father gets sick and dies. The mother walks for miles with her small children to ask the rich relatives for help. They mostly turn her away. The toddler grows up to be John of the Cross.
screen: `A MARRIAGE FOR LOVE.` → `CUT OFF BY THE FAMILY.` → `THE FATHER DIES YOUNG.`

segments.voice: First, hunger. John was born Juan de Yepes in 1542, in a small Castilian town called Fontiveros. His father, Gonzalo, died when John was very small. His mother, Catalina, kept the family alive by weaving, moving from town to town looking for work. It wasn't enough. One of John's brothers, Luis, died young, and some biographers think hunger was part of it. Second, the school. The family finally settled in Medina del Campo, a busy market town, and John was taken into a school for poor and orphaned children, where he got food, clothes and some learning. They tried to apprentice him to a trade: carpenter, tailor, woodcarver, painter. None of them stuck. Third, the hospital. As a teenager he worked in a hospital for the poor, a place for people with contagious diseases. He washed patients, fed them, cleaned up after them, and went out begging in the streets to pay for their care. People who knew him then remembered how gentle he was with the sick. Fourth, the choice. The hospital's director saw something in him and paid for him to study with the Jesuits. He offered John a secure future: become a priest and stay on as the hospital's chaplain. For a poor boy, that was everything. John said no, and quietly joined the Carmelites at twenty-one. The man who later wrote about nights and nothingness wasn't theorizing. He knew poverty, hunger and sickrooms first.
screen: `A HUNGRY CHILDHOOD.` · `A SCHOOL FOR POOR CHILDREN.` · `WASHING THE SICK AS A TEENAGER.` · `HE TURNS DOWN A SAFE FUTURE.` · then, large: `HE KNEW POVERTY FIRST.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who's sick right now, in body or in spirit: a friend in the hospital, a parent getting frail, a coworker who's been quietly struggling. If you pray, pray for them by name; if you don't, send them good attention. Then choose one small, concrete thing you could do for them: a text, a meal, a visit, a ride.
Hunger. What marked John of the Cross's childhood: a father's early death, a mother who wove for pennies, and a brother hunger may have taken too. Today's word.
Your line: he knew poverty first. Before the poems came the sickrooms. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics remember John of the Cross's early years of poverty and hospital work, and visiting the sick is one of the corporal works of mercy in Catholic teaching.

notes: Family history: Gonzalo de Yepes disinherited for marrying Catalina Álvarez, a poor weaver; Gonzalo died c. 1545; brother Luis died young (often attributed to malnutrition). Confirm; the script says 'many historians think hunger was part of it'.
The hook says three sons: Francisco, Luis and Juan. Confirm.
School: Colegio de la Doctrina in Medina del Campo; apprenticeships (carpenter, tailor, woodcarver, painter) per early biographers. Confirm.
Hospital de la Concepción (for contagious diseases, often called 'de las bubas'), director Alonso Álvarez de Toledo; the offer of ordination and a chaplaincy. Confirm.
Entered the Carmelites in 1563 at Medina del Campo, age 21. Confirm.
